name: Jeremy Bentham
summary: Founder of classical utilitarianism, Bentham judged laws and institutions by their effect on happiness. He opposed natural rights, the Anglican establishment, colonies and hereditary privilege, and argued for near-universal suffrage, secret ballot, publicity and free markets.

booksNotUsed.reason: Prison and surveillance design essays; they state no position on any quiz statement beyond what the Principles and SEP already give.
Not Paul, but Jesus is a religious polemic that takes no position on any quiz statement.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Constitutional Code rejects a hereditary legislature; Bentham also proposed abolishing titles of honour (SEP).

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Principles of Morals and Legislation: the question is not whether animals can reason but whether they can suffer.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Principles allows eating and painlessly killing animals but condemns tormenting them.

arbitrator-settles-disputes.rationale: He proposes a common court between nations but one with no coercive power, only publishing its opinion; a contingent for last-resort enforcement is mentioned as an option.

arms-reduction.rationale: Plan for a Universal and Perpetual Peace proposes reducing and limiting armed forces by treaty.

ban-interest.rationale: Defence of Usury argues no adult of sound mind should be hindered from making such bargain over money as he thinks fit; he opposes the usury laws.

collective-defense.rationale: The Plan for Universal Peace rejects treaties of alliance, offensive or defensive.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: The Plan for Universal Peace says to give up all colonies and found none; none are useful.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: SEP reports he rejected criminalising consensual sex and gave the first systematic defence of sexual liberty in English.

death-penalty.rationale: SEP reports he opposed the death penalty, dropping his exceptions by 1809.

democracy-best.rationale: Constitutional Code lays out a democratic constitution with the people holding supreme power.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Constitutional Code excludes women from legislative and executive office while giving them the franchise.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: He proposes a common court or congress of nations with only opinion-reporting powers; a contingent for last-resort enforcement is floated but not preferred.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: The Plan for Universal Peace says to make no treaties of alliance, offensive or defensive.

foreign-policy-non-interference.rationale: Emancipate Your Colonies urges reforming the world by example rather than by force and giving up distant dependencies.

free-trade.rationale: The Plan for Universal Peace holds all trade advantageous and bounties and prohibitions harmful.

free-trade-promotes-peace.rationale: The Plan for Universal Peace links commerce without restrictions with peace between nations.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Constitutional Code excludes women from legislative and executive office.

harm-principle.rationale: Principles of Morals and Legislation finds little reason to punish self-regarding conduct and says legislators over-restrict it.

humans-entitled-to-use-animals.rationale: Principles accepts killing animals for human use where it is painless, and condemns torment.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: SEP: laissez-faire is his default ("Be quiet") with limited exceptions; Defence of Usury argues for free contracts.

military-force-beyond-defence.rationale: Emancipate Your Colonies rejects conquest and reforming the world by force; the Plan for Peace treats aggressive war as a choice to avoid.

military-force-for-human-rights.rationale: Emancipate Your Colonies: "reform the world by force, you might as well reform the moon"; he urges reform by example.

military-superiority.rationale: The Plan for Universal Peace proposes limiting armed forces by treaty rather than seeking superiority over rivals.

national-church-status.rationale: Constitutional Code chapter "Established Religion — None" condemns a state church as an instrument of intimidation and corruption.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Anarchical Fallacies and the Fragment hold laws are to be obeyed and censured, not treated as void.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Civil Code argues marriage should not be an irrevocable bond where spouses come to hate each other, and supports liberty of divorce.

office-by-exam.rationale: SEP lists examinations to test officials' aptitude among his reforms.

open-government-data.rationale: Constitutional Code builds on publicity of official acts; SEP lists publicity among his securities against misrule.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Constitutional Code makes the supreme legislative not subordinate to any sub-legislature.

party-controls-media.rationale: His essay on the liberty of the press and public discussion argues for a free press and against laws that suppress it.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: He condemns unwritten, judge-made common law as a phantom and calls for enacted, published law (Plan of Parliamentary Reform and related works).

property-franchise.rationale: Plan of Parliamentary Reform proposes virtually universal suffrage, excluding only infants and the insane.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Constitutional Code and SEP describe publicity and open access to official information as securities against misrule.

publish-international-agreements.rationale: The Plan for Universal Peace requires treaties and negotiations to be public and rejects foreign-department secrecy.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Principles says blackness of skin is no reason to leave a human being without redress against a tormentor.

recall-officials.rationale: In the Constitutional Code the people hold a standing power to dismiss officials and legislators by petition and secret vote.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Constitutional Code gives the constituent body a power to dislocate legislators, exercised by secret vote.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Constitutional Code has the supreme legislative above the sub-legislatures and has a chapter on its powers over them.

rehabilitation.rationale: Principles lists reformation among the ends of punishment, alongside example and others; the Panopticon was reformative (SEP).

second-chamber.rationale: Constitutional Code argues for a single legislative chamber and lists the evils of two houses, rejecting a hereditary House of Lords.

separate-church-state.rationale: Constitutional Code provides for no established religion.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Constitutional Code has the husband's will decide in domestic disputes.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: The Plan for Universal Peace condemns commercial preference, bounties and prohibitions as harmful.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Emancipate Your Colonies calls conquest "vulgar ambition" and urges giving freedom to colonies instead of conquering.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Fragment on Government: "to obey punctually, to censure freely"; resistance only where utility favours it.

women-suffrage.rationale: Constitutional Code gives women an equal vote by secret ballot but excludes them from legislative and executive office.

notes: Bentham has no personal record; every answer is from his writings (words) and the SEP. Searched government, world, economy, liberty, society, ecology and technology. Statements the texts do not speak to are null. Works were read in the Bowring edition on archive.org.
